forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Bury faces £9.585m gap in 2027/28 budget after £10.747m of proposed savings
news_drafts.lead:
Bury Council's Cabinet on 14 October is presented with a refreshed medium-term financial strategy (MTFS, the council's multi-year plan setting expected spending against expected income). It shows a gap of £20.332m for 2027/28 before savings. The council proposes £10.747m of new savings, mainly by deleting vacant posts, redesigning services and changing policies. That leaves £9.585m, rising to a cumulative £17.508m by 2029/30.

The 2027/28 gap is £6.434m larger than the £13.898m set when the budget was approved in February 2026. Budget assumptions rose by £6.161m and expected funding fell by £0.273m. Demand and volume growth adds £4.084m, treasury and capital financing costs £3.094m, and the 6.4% rise in the Real Living Wage (the voluntary hourly pay rate set above the legal minimum) £1.482m. In-year budget monitoring (the check of spending against budget) forecasts a 2026/27 overspend of £5.691m, or 2.26% of the £252.135m net budget. Health and Adult Care accounts for £2.543m and Children and Young People £2.212m.

Money set aside to support the budget, the Budget Stabilisation Reserve, is forecast to fall from £15.599m at March 2026 to £5.977m at March 2027. That follows £3.977m of approved use this year and an estimated £5.691m to cover the overspend. The paper states: "The Council no longer has a sufficient Budget Stabilisation Reserve to fund the current budget gaps and therefore cannot rely upon reserves as a viable means of balancing future budgets."

findings.paper_title: 26 09Sept24 512795 Initial Budget Estimate Nr 4 CB V2
findings.headline: Pupil referral unit cost estimate £16,999,519 with identified cost range of £16.5m to £17.5m due to volatile construction market
findings.detail: Stage 3 cost estimate for new two-storey pupil referral unit at Ash Grove, Radcliffe with total anticipated client cost of £16,999,519. The document identifies material cost uncertainty due to energy prices and geopolitical factors, with an anticipated range of £16.5m to £17.5m. The estimate includes £1,516,600 risk allowance and £627,700 inflation allowance, but explicitly notes that market supply prices are rising faster than forecast indices and these increases are not reflected in the estimate.
findings.matters: Finance directors and lenders need visibility of capital project cost risks. A £1 million range (6%) on a £17 million project represents material uncertainty, and the explicit note that actual market inflation may exceed forecast assumptions is material to forward financial planning and borrowing decisions.
findings.figures: Total anticipated cost £16,999,519; cost range £16.5m-£17.5m; construction cost £11,994,400; risk allowance £1,516,600; inflation allowance £627,700; assumed tender inflation 1.92%, construction inflation 1.88%
findings.quote: The construction market is very volatile at present and costs are unpredictable due to energy prices and the wars in Ukraine and Iran. We would anticipate that this scheme could cost between £16.5m and £17.5m

findings.paper_title: 9. Cabinet report - New Lease 6B 6C Bridge Trading Estate (Oct 2026)
findings.headline: Bury's Adult Care Equipment Service cost of £5.11 per resident is mid-range for Greater Manchester peer services (£3.88-£6.90 range)
findings.detail: The council compared operating costs across Greater Manchester councils. Costs range from £3.88 to £6.90 per head. Bury at £5.11 per head is in the middle of this distribution. The lowest-cost councils operate from wholly council-owned buildings with negligible property costs; only two services operate this way.
findings.matters: Shows the council's unit costs are not exceptional given the cost of the premises, and that cost differences between councils are largely property-driven rather than reflecting service efficiency.
findings.figures: Bury £5.11 per person; GM range £3.88-£6.90; two councils operate from council-owned buildings
findings.quote: the cost of delivering the service here in Bury is £5.11 per person compared to a low of £3.88 and a high of £6.90

findings.paper_title: 9. Cabinet report - New Lease 6B 6C Bridge Trading Estate (Oct 2026)
findings.headline: No readily available alternative premises identified; relocation estimated at £160k in dilapidation costs with service disruption risk
findings.detail: Alternatives were considered: relocating the service or closing it. Both were rejected. No suitable alternative premises have been identified. The existing unit has £436,925 of 2015 capital investment plus £18,000 lift installation. Relocation would incur approximately £160k in dilapidation and reinstatement works plus new fit-out costs.
findings.matters: The council's options are constrained by prior capital investment and lack of alternatives, effectively forcing acceptance of the rent increase to avoid larger one-time costs and service disruption to an essential social care function.
findings.figures: Capital investment 2015 £436,925; lift installation £18,000; estimated dilapidation £160k; unit 11,395 sq ft
findings.quote: there are no readily available alternative premises currently identified that would provide an equivalent operational base

findings.paper_title: 9. Cabinet report - New Lease 6B 6C Bridge Trading Estate (Oct 2026)
findings.headline: Agreed rent of £8.95 per sq ft is within local market range; market comparison shows £8.00-£10.00 typical for secondary industrial space
findings.detail: The council tested the new rent against comparable industrial accommodation in Bury and North Manchester. Secondary industrial space typically ranges £8.00-£10.00 per sq ft; newer or higher specification premises exceed £11.00 per sq ft. The agreed rate is positioned at the lower end of that range.
findings.matters: Demonstrates the substantial cost increase reflects current market conditions rather than a punitive negotiated outcome, though it confirms the council has limited negotiating leverage.
findings.figures: Agreed £8.95 per sq ft; local market £8.00-£10.00; higher specification >£11.00 per sq ft; unit 1,058.69 sq m
findings.quote: The agreed rent of approximately £8.95 per sq ft is therefore considered to be within the range evidenced by the local market.

findings.paper_title: 9. Cabinet report - New Lease 6B 6C Bridge Trading Estate (Oct 2026)
findings.headline: Open market rent review on 18 May 2030 creates further cost uncertainty; same date as tenant-only break clause
findings.detail: The lease includes an open market rent review on 18 May 2030 when the rent will reset to the greater of the passing rent (£102,000) or the open market value. The council's break option (six months' notice required) is dated 17 May 2030, meaning the council's exit decision point coincides with potential for a further rent increase.
findings.matters: Creates material future cost uncertainty; market rent reviews typically increase with inflation, and the council's mitigation options converge at a single point five years into the lease.
findings.figures: Rent review and break clause both due May 2030; basis is greater of passing rent or open market rent
findings.quote: Rent review: open market rent review on 18 May 2030, with the reviewed rent being the greater of the passing rent or the open market rent determined in accordance with the lease.
